result.question: Which techniques most improve speech emotion recognition (4 classes: angry/happy/neutral/sad, macro-F1) on a very small Hindi dataset (826 train / 209 test clips, 1-11 s, about 30% noisy near-duplicates, source corpus BhavVaani)? The current system is a blend of logistic-regression probes on frozen Whisper-large-v3 and w2v-BERT-2.0 layers, Qwen2.5-Omni hidden states and zero-shot log-probs, an e5 transcript-text probe, and an attentive-pooling audio-text head. Already tried without gain: fine-tuning, emotion2vec, WavLM, CLAP, openSMILE, pseudo-labels, label spreading, kNN, stacking, calibration, audio-LLM zero-shot, external Indian SER data. Find evidence-backed ideas NOT in that list: Hindi/Indic SER papers and GitHub/Hugging Face code (2023-2026), prosody or behavioural features, better probe heads or layer fusion, and Kaggle small-audio-competition tactics. Only public, free models are allowed, and no human labels of test records may be used.
result.summary: The verified evidence answers the question only weakly. None of the 8 surviving claims shows a gain on Hindi, BhavVaani or any Indic data, and none was measured with macro-F1 on a dataset as small as 826 clips. The one actionable idea not already tried is speaker normalization: train the emotion head adversarially to remove speaker information (Gat et al., ICASSP 2022). This rests on the well-supported warning that small SER sets let classifiers learn speaker shortcuts. Its frozen-feature variant gained only +0.1 to +2.0 weighted accuracy on IEMOCAP, and the larger gains needed fine-tuning, which this project has already tried without success. A second idea is early audio-text fusion through multi-head attention plus a second attention pooling. It ranked 3rd of 31 teams at Odyssey 2024 (34.41% macro-F1, self-reported), but the project's existing attentive-pooling audio-text head already covers most of it, so at most an early-fusion multi-head-attention variant is worth testing. Every candidate tactic around these two was refuted or unverified: segmental pooling, augmentation recipes, jitter/shimmer prosody, neuron selection, and frozen-versus-fine-tuned results. Treat both ideas as hypotheses to pre-register under the grouped repeated CV, not as expected wins.

findings.claim: Small SER datasets can let classifiers learn speaker shortcuts. A speaker-adversarial (gradient-reversal) head that strips speaker information from the representation is a candidate untried technique. On frozen HuBERT-Large it improved IEMOCAP weighted accuracy from 71.9 to 73.9, but on HuBERT-Base the gain was only 69.0 vs 68.9. The larger gains came from a variant that fine-tunes the upstream model.
findings.evidence: Merged from claims 0, 1 and 5. The shortcut warning won 3-0. The method and its IEMOCAP SOTA claim won 2-1. The verifier read Table 1: on HuBERT-Large, a speaker-ID probe on the frozen features fell from 60.7% to 45.9% after normalization. Results are single-seed, IEMOCAP only and English only. Applying this to frozen Whisper or w2v-BERT probes is the reviewers' own extrapolation. It needs speaker or pseudo-speaker labels (for example, clusters of speaker embeddings), which this dataset does not provide.

findings.claim: Early fusion of self-supervised audio and text features through a multi-head-attention layer, followed by a second attention pooling to an utterance vector, placed 3rd of 31 teams in the Odyssey 2024 categorical SER task (34.41% macro-F1).
findings.evidence: Merged from claims 2 and 3. The architecture description won 3-0 and the ranking 2-1. The ranking is self-reported and was not checked against the organizers' leaderboard. The data is large English podcast speech (MSP-Podcast), not small Indic data. No ablations were verified because the PDF body could not be parsed. The project's attentive-pooling audio-text head already resembles this design, so the only new piece is to fuse audio and text tokens before attention instead of after.

findings.claim: Segmental average pooling (averaging only speech frames, combined with global pooling) has no verified evidence for Hindi. The paper tested only IEMOCAP and KEMDy19, and its SOTA claim was refuted 0-3.
findings.evidence: Claim 4 (2-1) confirms only that the paper's scope excludes Indic languages. It is still a cheap probe-side variant: mask out silence and padding frames before mean pooling. That may matter here because Whisper features are padded with trailing silence, but this is a hypothesis with no evidence behind it.

findings.claim: emotion2vec is pre-trained by self-supervised online distillation on about 262 h of unlabeled emotion data, with both utterance-level and frame-level losses. It is already excluded in this project, and the claim that its frozen linear probe beats specialist models was refuted 0-3.
findings.evidence: Claim 6, vote 2-1. The 262 h figure comes from a search snippet and was not read in the paper body. A 2025 third-party comparison found emotion2vec below WavLM-base on ESD and MELD. This gives no reason to revisit emotion2vec.

findings.claim: TextPro-SLM (2026), a prosody-aware speech LLM, claims strong paralinguistic understanding but reports no SER figures, so there is no evidence it would help here.
findings.evidence: Claim 7, vote 2-1. The source is an unreviewed preprint with a self-promotional abstract. It is listed only for completeness. Audio-LLM features (Qwen2.5-Omni) are already in the blend.

result.caveats: No surviving source evaluates Hindi, Indic or BhavVaani data, or a setting with near-duplicate noise. Every result comes from English or Korean benchmarks with weighted accuracy or large corpora, so transfer to 826 clips is untested. The biggest speaker-normalization gains need upstream fine-tuning, which has already failed in this project. Several leads promised in the research question found no verified support: Indic SER papers and code, prosody or jitter/shimmer features, layer-fusion or probe-head papers, and Kaggle small-audio tactics. Their candidate claims were refuted (17 refuted vs 8 confirmed). Some quotes were checked only through fetch summaries or abstracts, not full PDFs. Rankings and SOTA statements are self-reported and date from 2022-2024. Today is 2026-10-12, after the code-sharing embargo of 11 Oct; check GOAL.md to see whether the competition deadline still leaves time to run any experiment.
openQuestions: Does the 826-clip set have recoverable speaker structure, for example clusters of ECAPA or x-vector embeddings? If so, do near-dup-grouped folds still leak speakers, inflating CV, and would speaker-grouped folds or a speaker-adversarial probe change the ranking of blend members?
Does masking silence and padding frames before pooling (segmental pooling) help the padded Whisper and w2v-BERT layer probes under repeated grouped CV?
Does early token-level fusion of audio and text features with multi-head attention beat the existing late attentive-pooling audio-text head on 826 clips, or does it overfit?
Are there any published Hindi or BhavVaani SER baselines with speaker-independent macro-F1 to benchmark against? None surfaced in verified form.

refuted.claim: Frozen emotion2vec features with only a linear layer trained on top outperform state-of-the-art universal SSL models and emotion-specialist models on IEMOCAP. Central to the research question as a claim that a frozen-feature linear probe can beat fine-tuned specialists, though emotion2vec is already in the excluded-without-gain list for this project.

Segmental average pooling, which averages only speech segments and ignores non-speech frames, combined with global average pooling reaches state-of-the-art results on IEMOCAP (English). Quote is from the arXiv abstract page as relayed by the fetch tool, not verbatim.
Frozen self-supervised wav2vec-based features fed to a custom CNN classifier outperform a support vector machine baseline on the ShEMO dataset (Persian, not Hindi).
The same wav2vec-features-plus-CNN approach outperforms transfer learning with a pretrained CNN on ShEMO.
Large speech emotion datasets are hard to obtain, which motivates methods that cope with small, biased data. This matches the 826-clip Hindi setting.

The paper reports tests on 13 datasets covering 10 languages with consistent gains, which it presents as evidence of language generalization. The text I could extract does not mention Hindi or other Indic languages, so this is not direct evidence for Hindi. (Paraphrased, no quote.)

Adding three jitter/shimmer features (absolute jitter, shimmer in dB, shimmer apq3) to a 9-feature prosodic speaker-verification baseline improved its EER by about 17% relative. The paper is about speaker verification, not emotion, so this is transfer evidence only.

In the speaker-verification experiments, the absolute jitter and shimmer measures were more discriminant than their relative variants, and relative jitter measures added nothing when fused with the absolute measure. This suggests that for SER, absolute perturbation measures may be the ones worth extracting.

The paper reports that jitter and shimmer values can differ significantly between speaking styles, especially for shimmer, and cites prior work for this. For SER this is a caveat: perturbation features may shift across corpora or recording conditions, so they need to be checked on this dataset before being used.

Cross-corpus training with CREMA-D augmentation gives a reported +1.2% weighted accuracy for DistilHuBERT SER and a 32% reduction in cross-fold variance. The gain is small and is from a single unreviewed preprint with English corpora only.

The paper's augmentation recipe for SER is random gain from -18 dB to +6 dB, pitch shifting within plus or minus 2 semitones, polarity inversion, and low-amplitude Gaussian noise (paraphrased, no quote used).

The paper's production result of 75.48% WA comes from a random-shuffle 5% hold-out, which allows speaker or near-duplicate leakage. The paper's own speaker-independence argument contradicts this split, so the number should not be trusted as honest CV. This supports keeping the grouped folds in hcv.py (paraphrased, no quote used).

The paper is a 2024 arXiv preprint by Costa, India and Hernando; the full-text PDF could not be parsed, so ablations, per-model numbers and any small-data, Hindi, prosody or probe-head content are unverified.

Neuron-selection method matters: mean-deviation and contrast-based selectors find emotion-sensitive neurons with markedly stronger causal effects. This could guide which hidden units a probe or layer-selection step should use, but it was not tested as a probe improvement.

Stable emotion-sensitive neuron rankings need only modest identification data. The paper's evaluation sets use 200 to 500 utterances per emotion. This is the claim most relevant to the small-data setting, although the paper's pools are still far larger than 826 clips in total.
On a small audio emotion dataset, frozen Wav2Vec2 layers 6-12 outperformed end-to-end finetuning (score 0.207 vs 0.161) in the BLEMORE challenge system.
Finetuning about 95M parameters on roughly 2,456 samples overfits severely, which the authors give as the reason for the gap versus frozen features.
